claim: A duration code instructs stimulus-specific crosstalk between TLR4-activated canonical NF-κB pathway and lymphotoxin-β receptor (LTβR) induced non-canonical NF-κB signaling.
source: Our systems-level analyses identified a duration code that instructs stimulus specific crosstalk between TLR4-activated canonical NF-κB pathway and lymphotoxin-β receptor (LTβR) induced non-canonical NF-κB signaling.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and experimental validation showing that IKK2 activities sustained for more than 2 hr and NIK-IKK1 activities longer than 8 hr selectively participated in crosstalk.

claim: LTβR costimulation synergistically enhanced the late RelA/NF-κB response to TLR4.
source: Indeed, LTβR costimulation synergistically enhanced the late RelA/NF-κB response to TLR4 prolonging NF-κB target gene-expressions.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA showing augmented late RelA activity at 24 hr in LPS+αLTβR costimulation regime and quantitative RT-PCR showing enhanced late gene expressions.

claim: Concomitant LTβR signal targeted TLR4-induced newly synthesized p100 for processing into p52.
source: Concomitant LTβR signal targeted TLR4-induced newly synthesized p100, encoded by Nfkb2, for processing into p52 that not only neutralized p100 mediated inhibitions, but potently generated RelA:p52/NF-κB activity in a positive feedback loop.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing p52 generation and immunoprecipitation showing RelA:p52 complex formation during costimulation.

claim: p100 processing into p52 neutralized p100 mediated inhibitions.
source: Concomitant LTβR signal targeted TLR4-induced newly synthesized p100, encoded by Nfkb2, for processing into p52 that not only neutralized p100 mediated inhibitions, but potently generated RelA:p52/NF-κB activity in a positive feedback loop.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing relief of RelA from p100/IκBδ-mediated inhibition during crosstalk.

claim: p100 processing into p52 potently generated RelA:p52/NF-κB activity in a positive feedback loop.
source: Concomitant LTβR signal targeted TLR4-induced newly synthesized p100, encoded by Nfkb2, for processing into p52 that not only neutralized p100 mediated inhibitions, but potently generated RelA:p52/NF-κB activity in a positive feedback loop.
evidence: Supported by EMSA showing RelA:p52 dimer as a strong nuclear DNA binding activity and gene expression data showing enhanced inflammatory gene expressions.

claim: Nfkb2 connected lymphotoxin signal within the intestinal niche in reinforcing epithelial innate inflammatory RelA/NF-κB response to Citrobacter rodentium infection.
source: Finally, Nfkb2 connected lymphotoxin signal within the intestinal niche in reinforcing epithelial innate inflammatory RelA/NF-κB response to Citrobacter rodentium infection, while Nfkb2−/− mice succumbed to gut infections owing to stromal defects.
evidence: Supported by in vivo infection experiments showing weakened RelA activation in IECs from Nfkb2−/− mice and reduced chemokine expression.

claim: Nfkb2−/− mice succumbed to gut infections owing to stromal defects.
source: Finally, Nfkb2 connected lymphotoxin signal within the intestinal niche in reinforcing epithelial innate inflammatory RelA/NF-κB response to Citrobacter rodentium infection, while Nfkb2−/− mice succumbed to gut infections owing to stromal defects.
evidence: Supported by survival data showing mortality in Nfkb2−/− mice and bone marrow chimera experiments demonstrating stromal requirement.

claim: Signal integration via the pleiotropic NF-κB system enables tissue microenvironment derived cues in calibrating physiological responses.
source: In sum, our results suggest that signal integration via the pleiotropic NF-κB system enables tissue microenvironment derived cues in calibrating physiological responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data showing crosstalk between canonical and non-canonical pathways.

claim: Macrophages and dendritic cells present in different anatomic niche display heterogeneity in inflammatory signatures.
source: Indeed, macrophages and dendritic cells present in different anatomic niche display heterogeneity in inflammatory signatures (Iwasaki and Kelsall, 1999; Stout and Suttles, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CD40 is required for inflammatory gene expressions in endothelial cells.
source: Likewise, a requirement for CD40, primarily involved in B-cell maturation, in inflammatory gene expressions in endothelial cells was documented (Pluvinet et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lymphotoxin-β receptor (LTβR) is critical for innate immune responses.
source: Similarly, lymph node inducing lymphotoxin-β receptor (LTβR) was shown to be critical for innate immune responses (Spahn et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NF-κB family of transcription factors plays an essential role in activating pathogen-responsive gene-expression program in tissue-resident cells.
source: The NF-κB family of transcription factors plays an essential role in activating pathogen-responsive gene-expression program in tissue-resident cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about NF-κB function.

claim: In the canonical NF-κB pathway, inflammatory cues engage NEMO-IKK2 kinase complex to phosphorylate inhibitory IκB proteins.
source: In the canonical NF-κB pathway, inflammatory cues engage NEMO-IKK2 (NEMO-IKKβ) kinase complex to phosphorylate inhibitory IκB proteins, the major isoform being IκBα, bound to the cytoplasmic RelA:p50 NF-κB dimers.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about canonical NF-κB signaling.

claim: Signal-induced phosphorylation leads to proteasomal degradation of IκBs and release of RelA:p50 dimers into the nucleus.
source: Signal-induced phosphorylation leads to proteasomal degradation of IκBs and release of RelA:p50 dimers into the nucleus.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about canonical NF-κB signaling.

claim: Nuclear RelA dimers activate the expressions of pro-inflammatory chemokine and cytokine genes as well as its own inhibitor IκBα.
source: The nuclear RelA dimers activate the expressions of pro-inflammatory chemokine and cytokine genes as well as its own inhibitor IκBα, which ensures proper attenuation of inflammatory responses in a negative feedback loop.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about NF-κB target genes and negative feedback.

claim: IκBα ensures proper attenuation of inflammatory responses in a negative feedback loop.
source: The nuclear RelA dimers activate the expressions of pro-inflammatory chemokine and cytokine genes as well as its own inhibitor IκBα, which ensures proper attenuation of inflammatory responses in a negative feedback loop.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about NF-κB negative feedback regulation.

claim: Non-canonical signaling involves NIK and IKK1 mediated phosphorylation of Nfkb2 encoded precursor p100 bound to RelB.
source: In contrast to canonical signaling, the non-canonical pathway transduces signals from cell-differentiating cues those engage BAFFR, CD40, or LTβR. Non-canonical signaling involves NIK and IKK1 (NIK-IKKα) mediated phosphorylation of Nfkb2 encoded precursor p100 bound to RelB (Sun, 2012).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citation to prior literature.

claim: Proteasomal processing removes the C-terminal inhibitory domain of p100 from RelB:p100 complex to generate RelB:p52 NF-κB dimer.
source: Subsequent proteasomal processing removes the C-terminal inhibitory domain of p100 from RelB:p100 complex to generate RelB:p52 NF-κB dimer, which mediates the expressions of organogenic chemokine genes in the nucleus (Bonizzi et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citation to prior literature.

claim: RelB:p52 NF-κB dimer mediates the expressions of organogenic chemokine genes in the nucleus.
source: Subsequent proteasomal processing removes the C-terminal inhibitory domain of p100 from RelB:p100 complex to generate RelB:p52 NF-κB dimer, which mediates the expressions of organogenic chemokine genes in the nucleus (Bonizzi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In its homo-oligomeric form, termed IκBδ, p100 utilizes its inhibitory domain to sequester a subpopulation of the RelA:p50 dimer.
source: In its homo-oligomeric form, termed IκBδ, p100 was shown to utilize its inhibitory domain to sequester a subpopulation of the RelA:p50 dimer (Basak et al., 2007; Savinova et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LTβR through non-canonical NIK-IKK1 signal inactivates IκBδ to induce a weak yet sustained RelA:p50 activity.
source: LTβR through non-canonical NIK-IKK1 signal inactivates IκBδ to induce a weak yet sustained RelA:p50 activity.
evidence: Based on prior knowledge and experimental observations in the study.

claim: RelA-induced synthesis of p100 and consequent accumulation of inhibitory IκBδ exerts negative feedback limiting canonical RelA activity.
source: Conversely, RelA-induced synthesis of p100 and consequent accumulation of inhibitory IκBδ was shown to exert negative feedback limiting canonical RelA activity (de Wit et al., 1998; Legarda-Addison and Ting, 2007; Shih et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An alternate RelA:p52 dimer constitutes a minor kappaB DNA binding activity.
source: In addition, an alternate RelA:p52 dimer has been reported which is thought to constitute a minor kappaB DNA binding activity (Hoffmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IKK2 activities sustained for more than 2 hr are more likely to engage into crosstalk.
source: Plotting the dynamic features of the crosstalk-proficient kinase inputs, we could reveal a critical duration threshold; where IKK2 activities sustained for more than 2 hr were more likely to engage into crosstalk for varied peak amplitudes and inputs with shorter duration were crosstalk inefficient (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NIK-IKK1 activities longer than 8 hr selectively participated into crosstalk with the canonical pathway.
source: Illustrating a similar but more elaborate duration control, NIK-IKK1 activities longer than 8 hr selectively participated into crosstalk with the canonical pathway.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results.

claim: IL-1β only transiently activates IKK2 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: Consistent to the prior report (Werner et al., 2008), our kinase assay ('Materials and methods') revealed that IL-1β, an important pro-inflammatory cytokine, only transiently activates IKK2 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (left panel, Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1F and citation to prior literature.

claim: Bacterial LPS through TLR4-induced IKK2 activity persisted above the basal level even at 24 hr post-stimulation.
source: In contrast, bacterial LPS through TLR4-induced IKK2 activity that persisted above the basal level even at 24 hr post-stimulation (right panel, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) (Covert et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1F and citation to prior literature.

claim: LTβR engagement using agonistic αLTβR antibody led to sustained activation of the non-canonical NIK-IKK1.
source: Mimicking prolonged signaling during cell-differentiation processes, LTβR engagement using agonistic αLTβR antibody led to sustained activation of the non-canonical NIK-IKK1 (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Computational simulations revealed insulation of IL-1R signaling from LTβR-mediated crosstalk.
source: Using these experimental kinase activities as inputs, our computational simulations revealed insulation of IL-1R signaling from LTβR-mediated crosstalk (left panel, Figure 1H), but robust crosstalk between TLR4 and LTβR that amplified late RelA response upon costimulation (right panel, Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Computational simulations revealed robust crosstalk between TLR4 and LTβR that amplified late RelA response upon costimulation.
source: Using these experimental kinase activities as inputs, our computational simulations revealed insulation of IL-1R signaling from LTβR-mediated crosstalk (left panel, Figure 1H), but robust crosstalk between TLR4 and LTβR that amplified late RelA response upon costimulation (right panel, Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1H.

claim: IL-1R signal elicited strong RelA activity at 30 min in EMSA that was largely attenuated within 1 hr.
source: IL-1R signal, in parallel to transient IKK2 activation, elicited strong RelA activity at 30 min in EMSA that was largely attenuated within 1 hr, whereas, non-canonical LTβR signal only weakly induced RelA and RelB dimers those persisted even at 24 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Non-canonical LTβR signal only weakly induced RelA and RelB dimers that persisted even at 24 hr.
source: IL-1R signal, in parallel to transient IKK2 activation, elicited strong RelA activity at 30 min in EMSA that was largely attenuated within 1 hr, whereas, non-canonical LTβR signal only weakly induced RelA and RelB dimers those persisted even at 24 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LTβR costimulation was ineffective in augmenting IL-1 induced RelA activity.
source: Indeed, we were unable to detect any significant enhancement of RelA activity, relative to IL-1 induced peak, upon costimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Canonical TLR4 induced a temporally distinct RelA NF-κB activity with an early peak at 1 hr, subsequent descend and a progressively weakened late phase between 8 hr and 24 hr.
source: In comparison, canonical TLR4 induced a temporally distinct RelA NF-κB activity with an early peak at 1 hr, subsequent descend and a progressively weakened late phase between 8 hr and 24 hr (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Concomitant LTβR signal sustained NF-κB response triggered by TLR4.
source: Corroborating our mathematical prediction, concomitant LTβR signal sustained NF-κB response triggered by TLR4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Signal integration via the NF-κB system synergistically enhanced TLR4-induced late RelA activity at 24 hr in the costimulation regime.
source: Signal integration via the NF-κB system synergistically enhanced TLR4-induced late RelA activity at 24 hr in the costimulation regime with mostly unaltered RelB response relative to solitary LTβR engagement (Figure 2B, quantification and Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data and quantification shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: TLR4 sequentially engages MyD88 and Trif to produce extended IKK2 activity.
source: Sequentially engaging MyD88 and Trif, TLR4 was shown to produce extended IKK2 activity (Covert et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Trif-deficient MEFs only transiently activated IKK2 upon LPS treatment.
source: To determine if the observed stimulus specificity of crosstalk is indeed due to the duration of IKK2, we utilized Trif-deficient MEFs that only transiently activated IKK2 upon LPS treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LTβR was restricted from crosstalk with TLR4 in Trif-deficient cells.
source: Despite a functional non-canonical pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), LTβR was restricted from crosstalk with TLR4 in Trif-deficient cells (Figure 2E), thereby, suggesting a Trif-dependent mechanism that relies on the duration of canonical IKK2 in imparting stimulus specificity of crosstalk control.
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A Trif-dependent mechanism relies on the duration of canonical IKK2 in imparting stimulus specificity of crosstalk control.
source: Despite a functional non-canonical pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), LTβR was restricted from crosstalk with TLR4 in Trif-deficient cells (Figure 2E), thereby, suggesting a Trif-dependent mechanism that relies on the duration of canonical IKK2 in imparting stimulus specificity of crosstalk control.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trif-deficient cells lack crosstalk despite functional non-canonical pathway.

claim: IL-1 treatment rapidly induces the expressions of TNF, IP-10, and MIP-1α mRNAs within 1 hr with residual expressions at 24 hr post-stimulation.
source: Our analyses revealed that IL-1 treatment rapidly induces the expressions of TNF, IP-10, and MIP-1α mRNAs within 1 hr with residual expressions at 24 hr post-stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The levels of IL-1β and RANTES mRNAs were insensitive to IL-1 treatment.
source: The levels of IL-1β and RANTES mRNAs were insensitive to IL-1 treatment.
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Weak LTβR signal alone did not significantly induce the expressions of pro-inflammatory genes in MEFs.
source: Also, weak LTβR signal alone did not significantly induce the expressions of these pro-inflammatory genes in MEFs.
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LTβR costimulation was ineffective in augmenting IL-1 induced early or late expressions of chemokine and cytokine genes.
source: Indeed, LTβR costimulation was ineffective in augmenting IL-1 induced early or late expressions of the chemokine and cytokine genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Solitary LPS treatment robustly induced the expressions of TNF, IP-10, and MIP-1α mRNAs.
source: Solitary LPS treatment not only robustly induced the expressions of TNF, IP-10, and MIP-1α mRNAs, but also led to late accumulation of IL-1β and RANTES mRNAs at 24 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LPS treatment led to late accumulation of IL-1β and RANTES mRNAs at 24 hr.
source: Solitary LPS treatment not only robustly induced the expressions of TNF, IP-10, and MIP-1α mRNAs, but also led to late accumulation of IL-1β and RANTES mRNAs at 24 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LTβR costimulation prolonged TLR4-induced gene expressions with further augmented late expressions of IL-1β, IP-10, MIP-1α, and RANTES mRNAs.
source: Consistent to our hypothesis, LTβR costimulation prolonged TLR4-induced gene expressions with further augmented late, but not early, expressions of IL-1β, IP-10, MIP-1α, and RANTES mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TNF mRNA levels were insensitive to crosstalk regulation.
source: TNF mRNA levels were insensitive to crosstalk regulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Out of 943 LPS induced genes, 114 genes were further upregulated upon costimulation.
source: Out of 943 LPS induced genes, however, a select set of 114 genes was further upregulated upon costimulation.
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated an enrichment of NF-κB targets among genes positively controlled through crosstalk.
source: Strikingly, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) (Figure 3—source data 2, 'Materials and methods') demonstrated an enrichment of NF-κB targets among genes positively controlled through crosstalk (middle and top, Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rate constant associated with the NF-κB-induced transcription of Nfkb2 is the most critical parameter underlying crosstalk control of RelA NF-κB activity.
source: Our parameter sensitivity analysis identified the rate constant associated with the NF-κB-induced transcription of Nfkb2 as the most critical parameter underlying crosstalk control of RelA NF-κB activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by computational parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Nfkb2 precursor function in generating RelA:p52 dimer is important for augmenting RelA NF-κB activity during crosstalk in WT system.
source: Computationally simulating individual RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 nuclear activities in the LPS, αLTβR, or costimulation regimes, we could further suggest that the Nfkb2 precursor function in generating RelA:p52 dimer is important for augmenting RelA NF-κB activity during crosstalk in WT system (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Crosstalk is completely abrogated in Nfkb2−/− cells.
source: Consistently, our modeling analyses predicted complete abrogation of crosstalk in Nfkb2−/− cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LPS induces RelA NF-κB-driven transcription of Nfkb2 to produce p100.
source: Our biochemical studies revealed that LPS induces RelA NF-κB-driven transcription of Nfkb2 to produce p100 (top panel, Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which was shown to oligomerize as NF-κB inhibitory IκBδ (Savinova et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2009; Tao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and mRNA data shown in Figure 4C and citations to prior literature.

claim: p100 oligomerizes as NF-κB inhibitory IκBδ.
source: Our biochemical studies revealed that LPS induces RelA NF-κB-driven transcription of Nfkb2 to produce p100 (top panel, Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which was shown to oligomerize as NF-κB inhibitory IκBδ (Savinova et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2009; Tao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Concomitant LTβR signal utilized TLR4-induced, newly synthesized p100 to potently generate p52, thereby, neutralizing the inhibitory p100 function.
source: Concomitant LTβR signal instead utilized TLR4-induced, newly synthesized p100 to potently generate p52, thereby, neutralizing the inhibitory p100 function (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NIK-IKK1 signal relieves RelA from p100/IκBδ-mediated inhibition during crosstalk.
source: Our immunoprecipitation based analysis demonstrated that NIK-IKK1 signal relieves RelA from p100/IκBδ-mediated inhibition during crosstalk (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LTβR costimulation of MEFs for 24 hr produced approximately fourfold more RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer as compared to solitary LPS treatments.
source: Intriguingly, LTβR costimulation of MEFs for 24 hr also produced ∼fourfold more RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer as compared to solitary LPS treatments (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RelA:p52 dimer generated upon LTβR costimulation appears as a strong nuclear DNA binding activity at 24 hr.
source: In supershift assay, we could ascertain that RelA:p52 dimer generated upon LTβR costimulation appears as a strong nuclear DNA binding activity at 24 hr (Figure 4E) to supplement to the TLR4-induced RelA NF-κB responses.
evidence: Supported by supershift assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dimerization stabilizes NF-κB monomers from degradation.
source: An important role of dimerization in stabilizing NF-κB monomers from degradation has been reported earlier (Fusco et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: RelA protein rapidly accumulated in cells upon proteasome inhibition.
source: Interestingly, RelA protein rapidly accumulated in cells upon proteasome inhibition (Figure 4F) suggesting a robust constitutive degradation mechanism that offsets basal synthesis of RelA monomers in maintaining the steady-state level.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A robust constitutive degradation mechanism offsets basal synthesis of RelA monomers in maintaining the steady-state level.
source: Interestingly, RelA protein rapidly accumulated in cells upon proteasome inhibition (Figure 4F) suggesting a robust constitutive degradation mechanism that offsets basal synthesis of RelA monomers in maintaining the steady-state level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RelA accumulates upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: Canonical RelA:p50 response to TLR4 signal is largely intact in Nfkb2−/− with early induction and diminished late activities comparable to WT MEFs.
source: Next, our genetic analyses revealed that canonical RelA:p50 response to TLR4 signal, primarily controlled through classical IκBs, is largely intact in Nfkb2−/− with early induction and diminished late activities comparable to WT MEFs (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A lack of RelA:p52 dimer generation in Nfkb2−/− cells ablated LTβR-mediated enhancement of TLR4-induced late RelA DNA binding activity.
source: Consistent to the prediction based on computational modeling studies, a lack of RelA:p52 dimer generation in Nfkb2−/− cells, however, ablated LTβR-mediated enhancement of TLR4-induced late RelA DNA binding activity (Figure 4G) as well as crosstalk amplification of RelA target pro-inflammatory gene expressions (bottom panel, Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4G and gene expression data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A lack of RelA:p52 dimer generation in Nfkb2−/− cells ablated crosstalk amplification of RelA target pro-inflammatory gene expressions.
source: Consistent to the prediction based on computational modeling studies, a lack of RelA:p52 dimer generation in Nfkb2−/− cells, however, ablated LTβR-mediated enhancement of TLR4-induced late RelA DNA binding activity (Figure 4G) as well as crosstalk amplification of RelA target pro-inflammatory gene expressions (bottom panel, Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Costimulation of Relb−/− MEFs led to similar hyperactivation of LPS-induced late expressions of IL-1β, IP-10, and RANTES mRNAs as in WT cells.
source: Importantly, costimulation of Relb−/− MEFs led to similar hyperactivation of LPS-induced late expressions of IL-1β, IP-10, and RANTES mRNAs as in WT cells (compare top panel, Figure 4H with Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The precursor function encoded by Nfkb2 in generating RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer is critical for integrating lymphotoxin derived signals to the pro-inflammatory RelA NF-κB pathway.
source: Therefore, our analyses confirmed that the precursor function encoded by Nfkb2 in generating RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer is critical for integrating lymphotoxin derived signals to the pro-inflammatory RelA NF-κB pathway.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic and biochemical analyses in Nfkb2−/− and Relb−/− cells.

claim: LTβR costimulation led to the hyperactivation of LPS-induced expressions of chemokine and cytokine genes in an Nfkb2-dependent manner with only a minor role for Relb.
source: Our analyses also suggested that LTβR costimulation led to the hyperactivation of LPS-induced expressions of chemokine and cytokine genes in an Nfkb2-dependent manner with only a minor, if any, role for Relb.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of gene expression data in Nfkb2−/− and Relb−/− cells.

claim: LPS induced Nfkb2 mRNA with a delay as opposed to rapid expression of Nfkbia mRNA.
source: As opposed to rapid expression of Nfkbia mRNA, which encodes IκBα, LPS induced Nfkb2 mRNA with a delay (top panel, Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Chronic TNF treatment induced Nfkb2 mRNA in WT MEFs with an explicit 1 hr delay.
source: Similarly, chronic TNF treatment induced Nfkb2 mRNA in WT MEFs with an explicit 1 hr delay (Figure 5B) that was also observed earlier and incorporated in both the previous (Basak et al., 2007) as well as the current mathematical model versions.
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B and citation to prior work.

claim: When Nfkb2 transgene was stably expressed in Nfkb2−/− MEFs from an exogenous NF-κB responsive promoter, Nfkb2 mRNA was readily induced by TNF without a delay.
source: When Nfkb2 transgene was stably expressed in Nfkb2−/− MEFs from an exogenous NF-κB responsive promoter, Nfkb2 mRNA was readily induced by TNF without a delay (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IL-1 treatment was ineffective in activating the expression of Nfkb2 mRNA in WT MEFs, despite the early induction of Nfkbia.
source: Remarkably, IL-1 treatment was ineffective in activating the expression of Nfkb2 mRNA in WT MEFs, despite the early induction of Nfkbia (bottom, Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eliminating the transcriptional delay allowed the mathematical model to simulate Nfkb2 mRNA induction by IL-1 treatment.
source: Only upon eliminating the transcriptional delay, our mathematical model could simulate Nfkb2 mRNA induction by IL-1 treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The defect in Nfkb2 mRNA induction by IL-1 treatment was rescued in the engineered Nfkb2−/− cell line expressing Nfkb2 transgene from the NF-κB-responsive promoter without the delay.
source: Indeed, we could also experimentally rescue the defect in Nfkb2 mRNA induction by IL-1 treatment in the engineered Nfkb2−/− cell line, which expresses Nfkb2 transgene from the NF-κB-responsive promoter without the delay (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Disruption of NF-κB-inducible synthesis by expressing p100 from a constitutive promoter in Nfkb2−/− MEFs abrogated crosstalk amplification of TLR4-induced late NF-κB activity by concomitant LTβR signal.
source: Consistent to our computational identification that NF-κB inducible transcription of Nfkb2 is important, disruption of NF-κB-inducible synthesis by expressing p100 from a constitutive promoter in Nfkb2−/− MEFs abrogated crosstalk amplification of TLR4-induced late NF-κB activity by concomitant LTβR signal (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The NF-κB-responsive expression of Nfkb2 transgene in Nfkb2−/− cells restored the crosstalk effect at the level of RelA NF-κB activation.
source: While the NF-κB-responsive expression of Nfkb2 transgene in Nfkb2−/− cells restored the crosstalk effect at the level of RelA NF-κB activation (Figure 5E) by potentiating RelA:p52 induction in LPS+αLTβR costimulation regime (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5E and supershift analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A promoter intrinsic delay necessitates persistent canonical signal for RelA-mediated induction of pro-synergistic Nfkb2.
source: Our results confirmed that signal induction of Nfkb2 is important for crosstalk and suggested that a promoter intrinsic delay necessitates persistent canonical signal for RelA-mediated induction of pro-synergistic Nfkb2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transient IL-1 signaling fails to induce Nfkb2 while sustained LPS signaling does.

claim: The delay encoding insulated IL-1R signaling from crosstalk by restricting Nfkb2 mRNA expressions.
source: Such delay encoding insulated IL-1R signaling, which transiently activates IKK2 and RelA by restricting Nfkb2 mRNA expressions, and accounted for the abrogated crosstalk in Trif-deficient MEFs that transiently activated the NF-κB pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of transcriptional delay and transient signaling.

claim: Pretreatment of engineered cells with αLTβR for 8 hr and subsequent IL-1 stimulation potentiated p52 production and prolonged IL-1-induced RelA response.
source: Pretreatment of these engineered cells with αLTβR for 8 hr and subsequent IL-1 stimulation that effectively converged the non-canonical signal to IL-1-induced Nfkb2 feedback, potentiated p52 production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and prolonged IL-1-induced RelA response (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and EMSA data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Negative feedbacks by IκBα and p100/IκBδ coordinately terminate canonical TLR4 response.
source: Negative feedbacks by IκBα and p100/IκBδ coordinately terminate canonical TLR4 response.
evidence: Based on the mechanistic understanding developed in the study.

claim: In a positive feedback loop, non-canonical LTβR signal targets the newly synthesized p100 to potently generate p52 and RelA:p52 dimers in sustaining inflammatory RelA NF-κB responses.
source: But, Nfkb2 functions pro-synergistically upon costimulation; in a positive feedback loop, non-canonical LTβR signal targets the newly synthesized p100, abundantly produced by TLR4, to potently generate p52 and RelA:p52 dimers in sustaining inflammatory RelA NF-κB responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the mechanistic studies presented.

claim: RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 heterodimers share DNA binding and gene-expression specificities.
source: Importantly, RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 heterodimers were shown to share DNA binding and gene-expression specificities (Siggers et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RelA:p52 dimer has comparable efficiency in inducing the expression of Nfkb2 mRNA as the RelA:p50 dimer.
source: Our experimental data also indicated that RelA:p52 dimer has comparable efficiency in inducing the expression of Nfkb2 mRNA as the RelA:p50 dimer (Appendix-1, Appendix figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Appendix figure 4C.

claim: The transcriptional delay intrinsic to the Nfkb2 promoter is critical for the duration code and stimulus specificity.
source: Although, emergent crosstalk is expected to be controlled by several biochemical constrains, the transcriptional delay intrinsic to the Nfkb2 promoter appears to be critical for the duration code and thereby the stimulus specificity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined computational and experimental analyses of Nfkb2 expression dynamics.

claim: Disruption of LTβR signal using LTβR-Ig fusion protein compromised innate immune responses upon subsequent infection with C. rodentium, leading to mortality.
source: Disruption of LTβR signal using LTβR-Ig fusion protein was shown to compromise innate immune responses upon subsequent infection with C. rodentium, a natural mouse enteric pathogen that led to mortality (Spahn et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IEC-specific deletion of LTβR obliterated bacterial clearance.
source: IEC-specific deletion of LTβR similarly obliterated bacterial clearance (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The engagement of ligand-expressing RORγt+ innate lymphoid cell provides the critical lymphotoxin signal in colon during the course of bacterial infection.
source: The engagement of ligand-expressing RORγt+ innate lymphoid cell is thought to provide the critical lymphotoxin signal in colon during the course of bacterial infection (Upadhyay and Fu, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A requirement of epithelial RelA activity in the chemokine gene expressions has been documented.
source: A requirement of epithelial RelA activity in the chemokine gene expressions has been documented earlier (Alcamo et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A functional non-canonical pathway downstream of LTβR augmented the RelA activity induced by pathogen sensing TLR4 in MSIE colon epithelial cell-line.
source: First, a functional non-canonical pathway downstream of LTβR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) augmented the RelA activity induced by pathogen sensing TLR4 in otherwise hypo-responsive MSIE colon epithelial cell-line (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Upon colonization, Citrobacter initially triggered epithelial accumulation of p100 that was fully processed into p52 by day5 in control-Ig treated mice.
source: Upon colonization, Citrobacter initially triggered epithelial accumulation of p100 that was fully processed into p52 by day5 (Figure 6B) generating RelA:p52 dimer (Figure 6C) in control-Ig, but not LTβR-Ig, treated mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Bacterial infection elicited RelA DNA binding activity in IECs that gradually accumulated in the nucleus with substantial contribution from RelA:p52 dimer at day5 post-infection.
source: Bacterial infection elicited RelA DNA binding activity in IECs that gradually accumulated in the nucleus (Figure 6D,E) with substantial contribution from RelA:p52 dimer along with RelA:p50 dimer at day5 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6D,E and supershift analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Exclusively RelA/NF-κB dimers are activated in IECs derived from mice infected with C. rodentium.
source: Our supershift analyses further confirmed complete absence of RelB containing NF-κB DNA binding activity in IECs derived from infected mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by supershift analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Perturbing LTβR signal attenuated RelA NF-κB activation with more obvious defects at day5.
source: Perturbing LTβR signal attenuated RelA NF-κB activation with more obvious defects at day5 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pathogen-responsive RelA activation in IECs derived from Nfkb2−/− mice was severely weakened at day5.
source: Likewise, pathogen-responsive RelA activation in IECs derived from Nfkb2−/− mice was severely weakened at day5 (Figure 6F) that led to significantly reduced expressions of the RelA target chemokines encoding KC and MIP-2α as compared to WT mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 6F and gene expression data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Weakened RelA activation in Nfkb2−/− IECs led to significantly reduced expressions of KC and MIP-2α as compared to WT mice.
source: Likewise, pathogen-responsive RelA activation in IECs derived from Nfkb2−/− mice was severely weakened at day5 (Figure 6F) that led to significantly reduced expressions of the RelA target chemokines encoding KC and MIP-2α as compared to WT mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Infected Nfkb2−/− mice exhibited diminished neutrophil recruitment in the lamina propria.
source: Indeed, infected Nfkb2−/− mice exhibited diminished neutrophil recruitment in the lamina propria, as revealed by anti-myeloperoxidase immunostaining of the colon sections (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Sustained epithelial RelA activity relies on LTβR mediated processing of pathogen-induced p100 into p52.
source: Sustained epithelial RelA activity that relies on LTβR mediated processing of pathogen-induced p100 into p52, therefore, mirrored our MEF-based analyses depicting crosstalk between canonical and non-canonical signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the in vivo infection data showing p100 processing and RelA activation.

claim: Subdued epithelial NF-κB activation in IECs from infected Nfkb2−/− mice suggested that a dominant precursor function of p100 supplying RelA:p52 dimer prolongs RelA response within the intestinal niche.
source: Subdued epithelial NF-κB activation, and not hyper-induction, in IECs from infected Nfkb2−/− mice also suggested that a dominant precursor function of p100 supplying RelA:p52 dimer prolongs RelA response within the intestinal niche.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nfkb2−/− mice show reduced, not increased, NF-κB activation.

claim: WT mice efficiently eliminated C. rodentium infections.
source: While WT mice efficiently eliminated infections, increased fecal excretion of bacteria at day10 post-infection in Nfkb2−/− mice (Figure 7A) indicated an inadequacy in limiting local infection, thereby, correlating with the observed defects in the early innate inflammatory response in this knockout (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by bacterial titer data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Nfkb2−/− mice showed increased fecal excretion of bacteria at day10 post-infection indicating an inadequacy in limiting local infection.
source: While WT mice efficiently eliminated infections, increased fecal excretion of bacteria at day10 post-infection in Nfkb2−/− mice (Figure 7A) indicated an inadequacy in limiting local infection, thereby, correlating with the observed defects in the early innate inflammatory response in this knockout (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by bacterial titer data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Infected Nfkb2−/− mice showed exacerbated damage with signatures of submucosal leukocyte infiltration.
source: Histological analysis of the shrunken colons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B) derived from the infected Nfkb2−/− mice further revealed exacerbated damage with signatures of submucosal leukocyte infiltration (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Breach in the intestinal barrier was accompanied by systemic bacterial dissemination with increased count in blood and liver.
source: Breach in the intestinal barrier was accompanied by systemic bacterial dissemination with increased count in blood (left panel, Figure 7C) and liver (right, Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Bacterial colitis induced in Nfkb2−/− mice resulted in significant body weight loss.
source: Finally, bacterial colitis induced in Nfkb2−/− mice resulted in significant body weight loss (Figure 7D) and onset of mortality as early as day10 post-infection (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Bacterial colitis induced in Nfkb2−/− mice resulted in onset of mortality as early as day10 post-infection.
source: Finally, bacterial colitis induced in Nfkb2−/− mice resulted in significant body weight loss (Figure 7D) and onset of mortality as early as day10 post-infection (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: WT bone marrow cells in Nfkb2−/− recipients were unable to prevent the infection-related colon pathology.
source: WT bone marrow cells in Nfkb2−/− recipients (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) were unable to prevent the infection-related colon pathology (Figure 7F), reductions in the body weight (Figure 7G) and morality (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by histological, body weight, and survival data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: WT recipients receiving either WT or Nfkb2−/− bone marrow resolved infections with comparable efficiencies.
source: In contrast, WT recipients receiving either WT or Nfkb2−/− bone marrow resolved infections with comparable efficiencies (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: Supported by histological, body weight, and survival data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: The protective function of Nfkb2 lies within stromal cells.
source: Our inability to rescue the infection-related mortality in Nfkb2−/− mice using WT hematopoietic cells indicated that the protective function of Nfkb2 lies within stromal cells.
evidence: Inferred from bone marrow chimera experiments showing that WT bone marrow cannot rescue Nfkb2−/− recipients.

claim: Adult mice lacking IgA or its transporter pIgR efficiently resolved Citrobacter infections.
source: Interestingly, adult mice, similar to those utilized in our study, lacking IgA or its transporter pIgR efficiently resolved Citrobacter infections (Maaser et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: μMT mice depleted of peripheral B-cells presented few mucosal changes in the first 2 weeks of infection and were completely free of mortality.
source: μMT mice depleted of peripheral B-cells presented few mucosal changes in the first 2 weeks of infection and were completely free of mortality (Simmons et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Rag1−/− mice succumbed to Citrobacter only late during infections in the 4th week.
source: Finally, Rag1−/− mice succumbed to Citrobacter only late during infections in the 4th week (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The stromal requirement of Nfkb2 lies within the intestinal epithelial cells in the initial events controlling early innate immunity.
source: Though, our study does not rule out crosstalk independent engagement of the Nfkb2 pathway in activating RelB:p52 dimer in the hematopoietic compartment at a later stage of infection, epithelial RelA NF-κB activation defects coupled to aggravated early colon pathology and early onset of mortality in Nfkb2−/− mice suggested that the stromal requirement of Nfkb2, at least in part, lies within the intestinal epithelial cells in the initial events controlling early innate immunity and involves crosstalk regulation of RelA NF-κB activity (Figure 7I, also discussed later).
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of epithelial defects, early pathology, and bone marrow chimera results.

claim: The pleiotropic NF-κB system enables tuning of cellular response to an instructive signal by microenvironment-derived additional costimulatory signals.
source: The NF-κB system transduces signals from a variety of cell-activating stimuli. Our study suggested that such pleiotropic system enables tuning of cellular response to an instructive signal by microenvironment-derived additional costimulatory signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: A duration code selectively integrates costimulatory LTβR signal with the TLR4 pathway, insulating transient cytokine signaling from crosstalk amplifications.
source: However, a duration code selectively integrates costimulatory LTβR signal with the TLR4 pathway, insulating transient cytokine signaling, secondary to microbial infections, from crosstalk amplifications.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the mechanistic studies showing stimulus-specific crosstalk.

claim: Positive feedback regulations underlie dose threshold control of NF-κB response in B-cells.
source: Recent studies have identified important positive feedback regulations underlying dose threshold control of NF-κB response in B-cells (Shinohara et al., 2014) or in myeloid cells (Sung et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A positive feedback loop sustains NF-κB response where non-canonical LTβR signal prolongs canonical TLR4 response by targeting RelA induced p100 for the generation of RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer.
source: Our crosstalk study illuminated a role of a positive feedback loop in sustaining NF-κB response; where non-canonical LTβR signal prolonged canonical TLR4 response by targeting RelA induced p100 for the generation of RelA:p52 NF-κB dimer.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the mechanistic studies presented.

claim: A dominant precursor function of p100 in producing RelA:p52 led to ablated crosstalk in Nfkb2−/− cells.
source: Indeed, a dominant precursor function of p100 in producing RelA:p52 led to ablated crosstalk in Nfkb2−/− cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic analyses in Nfkb2−/− cells.

claim: Non-canonical signal generates RelB:p52 by removing the C-terminal domain of p100 present in the preexisting RelB:p100 dimeric complex.
source: As such, non-canonical signal generates RelB:p52 by removing the C-terminal domain of p100 present in the preexisting RelB:p100 dimeric complex (Sun, 2012) or liberates RelA:p50 dimer from the p100/IκBδ-inhibited complexes (Basak et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-canonical signal liberates RelA:p50 dimer from the p100/IκBδ-inhibited complexes.
source: As such, non-canonical signal generates RelB:p52 by removing the C-terminal domain of p100 present in the preexisting RelB:p100 dimeric complex (Sun, 2012) or liberates RelA:p50 dimer from the p100/IκBδ-inhibited complexes (Basak et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Signal generation of the RelA:p52 dimer requires both canonical induction of p100/Nfkb2 expressions and concomitant processing of the newly synthesized p100 into p52 by non-canonical signal.
source: Signal generation of the RelA:p52 dimer requires both canonical induction of p100/Nfkb2 expressions and concomitant processing of the newly synthesized p100 into p52 by non-canonical signal.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the mechanistic studies showing requirement for both signals.

claim: p100 could be efficiently processed cotranslationally.
source: Previous report demonstrating that p100 could be efficiently processed cotranslationally (Mordmüller et al., 2003) explained the requirement of canonical signals in amply synthesizing nascent p100 as a substrate for the abundant production of p52 subunit during crosstalk.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mature p52 could readily dimerize with RelA, despite a preference of full-length p100 for RelB binding.
source: More so, mature p52 could readily dimerize with RelA, despite a preference of full-length p100 for RelB binding (Fusco et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is a significant overlap between RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 dimers in DNA binding.
source: Nevertheless, consistent to the observed gene-effect of crosstalk in our study, a significant overlap between RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 dimers in DNA binding (Siggers et al., 2012) and pro-inflammatory gene expressions (Hoffmann et al., 2003) was reported earlier.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a significant overlap between RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 dimers in pro-inflammatory gene expressions.
source: Nevertheless, consistent to the observed gene-effect of crosstalk in our study, a significant overlap between RelA:p50 and RelA:p52 dimers in DNA binding (Siggers et al., 2012) and pro-inflammatory gene expressions (Hoffmann et al., 2003) was reported earlier.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TLR4 activation of epithelial RelA was implicated in the chemokine gene expressions and neutrophil recruitment upon bacterial infections.
source: TLR4 activation of epithelial RelA was implicated in the chemokine gene expressions and neutrophil recruitment upon bacterial infections (Khan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Epithelial LTβR is important for effective innate immune responses to Citrobacter.
source: Yet, epithelial LTβR (Wang et al., 2010) was also important for effective innate immune responses to Citrobacter.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: LTβR provides a critical costimulatory signal through Nfkb2 to sustain RelA NF-κB response to pathogens in colonic epithelial cells.
source: In our proposed model (Figure 7I), we could clarify that LTβR provides a critical costimulatory signal through Nfkb2 to sustain RelA NF-κB response to pathogens in otherwise hyporesponsive colonic epithelial cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the in vivo infection studies.

claim: Signal integration ameliorated innate immune functions by enhancing pro-inflammatory gene expressions.
source: Such signal integration ameliorated innate immune functions by enhancing pro-inflammatory gene expressions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the gene expression and functional studies.

claim: p100−/− mice revealed hyperplasia of gastric epithelial cells and elevated expressions of RelA target genes.
source: Interestingly, p100−/− mice, which lacked the expression of p100, but aberrantly produced p52, revealed hyperplasia of gastric epithelial cells and elevated expressions of RelA target genes (Ishikawa et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In Nlrp12−/− mice, robust p52 generation in stromal cells through the non-canonical pathway led to colon cancer associated inflammation.
source: In Nlrp12−/− mice, robust p52 generation in stromal cells through the non-canonical pathway led to colon cancer associated inflammation (Allen et al., 2012), a hallmark for aberrant RelA activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: LTβR engagement in the dendritic cells within colonic patches triggered IL-22 production by innate lymphoid cells involving cell–cell communications to potentiate gut immunity.
source: LTβR engagement in the dendritic cells within colonic patches was shown to trigger IL-22 production by innate lymphoid cells involving cell–cell communications to potentiate gut immunity (Tumanov et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The epithelial requirement of LTβR is in sustaining RelA NF-κB response during bacterial infection.
source: Although, a defect in the colonic patches in Nfkb2−/− mice could impair IL-22 mediated protective responses, our cell-intrinsic crosstalk model explained that the reported epithelial requirement of LTβR (Wang et al., 2010) is in sustaining RelA NF-κB response during bacterial infection.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the mechanistic studies and in vivo infection data.

claim: Cell-differentiating cues present in the tissue microenvironment may play a more direct role in calibrating innate immune responses by engaging into cell-autonomous signaling crosstalks.
source: It extends the intriguing possibility that cell-differentiating cues present in the tissue microenvironment may play a more direct role, separate from merely determining the differentiation states of the resident cells, in calibrating innate immune responses by engaging into cell-autonomous signaling crosstalks.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.
